job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Marco Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in accounts payable at Dunmore Freight, a trucking and warehouse company out by the ring road. Each morning I get a pile of supplier invoices, match them against purchase orders and book them into the system, and my supervisor Brenda signs off on payments on Thursdays. I did my accounting degree at a city university and finished top of my class, mostly by being methodical. Evenings I cook for the two guys I share a house with, and on Sundays I do the books for my grandmother's noodle restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about right, it sounds like every tech wave that was supposed to change everything. I'd tell the guys at work that we've had new software before and the invoices still come in. I wouldn't be online about it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine and I'd be glad. I like my routine, and if the machines turn out to be mostly noise, my routine stays exactly what it is. I don't use any of the AI tools and I've never seen a reason to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep learning the system we have, and work towards a chartered accountancy certificate over the next three years. I'd keep saving about £150 a month. And I'd keep doing my grandmother's books on Sundays, because it's easy money and good practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. It's the one where I can sleep. I don't love the idea of constant change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or worry in your own life would stay exactly the same even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, the car loan and a student loan that's still about £9,000. I'm paid a normal graduate wage, so it's fine but it isn't loose. Brenda said the freight market is soft this year, which is the real thing on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your week is routine screen work that even a small change could touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, to be honest. Most of the invoices are routine matching, and even small tools can take a bite out of that. If Dunmore adds a scanner that reads invoices, I'd be watching to see how many of us still match them by hand.

say: I'd tell colleagues it sounds like **every tech wave** before.
I'd say we've had new software before and the **invoices** still come in.
think: I'm glad, because my **routine** stays the same.
I don't use **AI tools** and see no reason to start.
The soft **freight market** worries me more than software.
do: Keep learning the current **system** and aim at a chartered certificate.
Keep doing my grandmother's **restaurant books** on Sundays.
feel: **Settled**, the one picture where I sleep well.
S0.quote: I like my routine, and if the machines turn out to be mostly noise, my routine stays exactly what it is.
fieldNote: His unease comes from the **freight market** and loan, not AI.
Pride in **routine**; sees change as a cost.
Never used AI tools, so he judges them from **habit**.

steps.text: Work towards a chartered accountancy certificate over three years
Save £150 a month toward the student loan
Keep matching invoices accurately and on time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see how it goes, and I'd keep my head down. If someone asks, I'd say I don't love relying on software I can't check. With friends I'd say it's the kind of thing that moves too fast to judge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried. Matching invoices is what I do, and a program that reads an invoice and matches it to an order is exactly what a software company sells. I'm the kind of person who learns a tool two years after everyone else, and that could be the two years that matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Brenda about what the team should learn and ask to be trained before they roll anything out. I'd try one of the tools, probably the one Dunmore buys, because I'd rather be forced than guess. I'd also ask my grandmother if I could take over more of the restaurant's admin, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit grumpy. I know I should be excited, but I'm not. I just feel the ground move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think of a task you did last week. Which part would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three-way matching: invoice, order, delivery note. I do about eighty a day. If the software does that, my job becomes handling the odd ones, the disputes and the late payers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your manager do differently about hiring people at your level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd stop replacing people who leave. There were six of us two years ago and now there are five. A manager like Brenda wouldn't say it out loud, but the target is one person fewer each year.

I'd say I don't love relying on software I **can't check**.
I'd tell friends it moves too fast to **judge**.
think: Matching invoices is what I do, and software can do it, so I'm **worried**.
I learn tools **late**, and that could be the years that matter.
The team went from six to five without being **announced**.

Try the tool Dunmore buys, since I'd rather be **forced**.
Take over more of my grandmother's **restaurant** admin.
feel: **Uneasy** and grumpy, as if the ground is moving.
Annoyed that I'm **supposed** to be excited.
S1.quote: I'm the kind of person who learns a tool two years after everyone else, and that could be the two years that matter.
fieldNote: He names his own **lateness** with tools as the real risk.
The team shrinking from six to five is a **concrete** sign he reads well.
His fall-back is **family**, not a new field.

steps.text: Ask Brenda for training before any new invoice software arrives
Take over more of the noodle restaurant's admin
Ask my grandmother's accountant to share her client list
Watch how many invoice clerks Dunmore replaces this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is crazy and nobody can plan for that. At work I'd say nothing, because I'd be afraid of being the first named. With friends I'd say I think the government has to step in, but I'd have no idea how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be frightened. If a machine can do any desk job better and cheaper, a hundred graduates like me are competing with something that never sleeps and never asks for a rise. I wouldn't know what I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm not sure I'd do the right thing. I'd probably freeze for a month, then cut everything, stop the car loan extras and put every pound into savings. I'd talk to my parents about moving back home, and I'd ask my grandmother if I could work in the restaurant full time for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, and a bit numb. I've followed the rules, I did the degree. It feels like the rules got changed after I'd done my homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say it's the day the announcement is made. What do you tell the people close to you that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum and dad in the kitchen and say it's not my fault. They'd say come home and eat. Mum would cry a little, and dad would say the restaurant needs me anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what happens to the money you owe and the money you've saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car goes, because the loan is £220 a month. I'd sell it and use the bus. I'd keep the student loan at the minimum, and I'd hold about five months of cash, if I could get there.

I'd say **nothing** at work, afraid of being the first named.
I'd say the government has to **step in**, with no idea how.
think: A machine that never sleeps competes with every graduate, and I'd not know what I'm **for**.

do: Cut everything and save every **pound** towards five months of cash.
Sell the **car** and use the bus.
Move back to my parents or work at the **restaurant** full time.
feel: Hurt that the **rules changed** after I did my homework.
S2.quote: If a machine can do any desk job better and cheaper, a hundred graduates like me are competing with something that never sleeps and never asks for a rise.
fieldNote: Admits he might **freeze** first, which is rare candour.
Goes for **family** and the restaurant as his floor.
Sees the **fairness** problem more than the technology.

steps.text: Sell the car and use the bus to save £220 a month
Hold five months of cash and pay only the loan minimum
Move back home to my parents for a year
Ask my grandmother for full-time hours at the restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more reasonable, but I'd still be worried. At work I'd ask if the company has a plan for my team. I'd say we should get proper training and not be told to learn it at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be less frightened than at two years but still uneasy. I'd be 27 and maybe a senior accounts payable person, if my team still exists. With five years I can retrain slowly, but I'd have to start and I'm not great at starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my accountancy certificate by year three. I'd start using the tools in small ways, like the one that reads scanned invoices, so I'm not caught off guard. And I'd keep helping my grandmother and maybe pick up two or three small business clients on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but I can live with it. There's a dull ache more than panic. I worry I'd do nothing and wake up in year four with no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your plan with 5 years instead of 2?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be clear: the certificate first, the tools second, the clients third. With two years I'd be cutting and hiding. With five I can build one extra income and one new skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you do you think sees this coming, and who doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda sees it, and she's near retirement so she's calm. The younger staff at Dunmore mostly don't think about it. My friend Joon, who is in sales, says every year something is going to change everything.

say: I'd ask if the company has a **plan** for my team.
I'd say we need proper **training** at work, not at home.
I'd say five years is more **reasonable**, but still worrying.
think: Less frightened than at two years, but still **uneasy**.
I could retrain, but I'm **not great at starting**.
I fear doing **nothing** and waking up in year four.

Use the invoice-reading **tools** in small ways.
Pick up two or three small **business clients**.
S3.quote: With five years I can retrain slowly, but I'd have to start and I'm not great at starting.
fieldNote: He knows his **inertia** is the risk and states a plan to beat it.
The order of his plan: certificate, tools, **clients**.
Sees **older** staff as calm because they're near retirement.

steps.text: Finish the chartered accountancy certificate by year three
Use the scanned-invoice reader at work from next month
Find three small business clients for bookkeeping
Keep saving £150 a month toward a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let me read the next one, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and I'd stop worrying so much. At work I'd say the company has years to sort itself out. With friends I'd say we should use the time to learn something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, perhaps in a small finance team or with my own clients. I'd still not love the tools, but I'd learn them by then because I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate, then go for the next level. I'd learn one tool a year, slowly. And I'd save for a deposit on a small flat, because owning something solid helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little guilt because I know I'd drift, but a decade is long. I'd feel I could win the long game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what would you start now that you wouldn't with 2 years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the dull but useful things, the ones that don't need a clever plan. A decade is long enough for a slow person like me to catch up, so long as I start the slow part now. With two years I couldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At 32, what do you hope your working life looks like, and what could stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to run a small practice or be a finance lead at a mid-size firm. What could stop me is a recession, or the whole accounts function being replaced by software in a way nobody notices until it has gone.

S4.quote: A decade is long enough for a slow person like me to catch up, so long as I start the slow part now.
fieldNote: A decade lets his **slow** style fit the pace of change.
He wants something **solid**, a flat and a practice.
The fear left is a **quiet** replacement of whole functions.

steps.text: Pass the next-level accountancy exams by 2031
Learn one new accounting tool each year
Save £200 a month for a flat deposit
Buy a small flat in my own town by 2034

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be freezing and cutting at the same time. What would help is a clear plan from my firm about what happens to my team, training during work hours, and some kind of floor if it goes badly. And I'd want it written down, not just promised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that I'm not against change, I'm just slow to trust it. Slow people still have rent to pay, and nobody planning the future seems to count us. That's what I'd want someone to hear.

headlineQuote: Slow people still have rent to pay, and nobody planning the future seems to count us.
portrait: Marco is a **22-year-old** accounts payable graduate at a freight firm, top of his class, who prefers routine and never uses AI.
He is pragmatic and centrist, blames **no one in particular**, and wants clear plans and training.
His real risk is being **late** to tools, and he says so himself.
He feels uneasy in the mild case, **alarmed** at two years, and falls back on his family's restaurant.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, where he might freeze and have no time to learn.
whatWouldHelp: A written **plan** from his firm, training in work hours, and a floor if it goes badly.
